theme: If the LORD had not been on our side
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 124 and Psalm 125 slowly, twice. Both are Psalms of Ascent. Psalm 124 looks back at past deliverance; Psalm 125 looks forward in confident trust. Together they are the song of those who have walked through hardship and arrived at certainty about who God is.
settingTheScene: We continue the Psalms of Ascent. Psalm 124 is attributed to David and reflects on what would have happened to Israel if the LORD had not been on their side. Psalm 125 then offers confident trust, those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved. Together they capture both the memory and the hope of God’s people. They are perfect songs for those who have made it through difficulty and are walking by faith toward the future.
observation: Psalm 124 opens with a hypothetical: “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side…”, followed by vivid pictures of what would have happened.
The threats described are dramatic: men rising up, being swallowed alive, the floods sweeping us away, the torrent going over our soul.
Verse 6 turns to praise: “Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth!”
The bird-and-snare image (verse 7) captures the suddenness of God’s deliverance.
The psalm closes with the same confession as Psalm 121:2, “Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.”
Psalm 125:1 opens with a simile: “Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved.”
Verse 2: “As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people, from this time forth and forevermore.”
The psalm acknowledges the threat of evil (the “scepter of wickedness”) but promises it will not “rest on the land allotted to the righteous.”
It closes with the prayer: “Peace be upon Israel!”
interpretation:
These two short psalms complement one another. The first remembers past rescue. The second confidently anticipates future stability. Together they form the bipolar prayer of the believer: gratitude for what God has done, confidence in what God will do.

Psalm 124 begins with one of the most striking rhetorical devices in the Psalter. “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side…” And then the psalmist runs through the disasters that would have followed: enemies would have swallowed them alive, floods would have swept them away, torrents would have gone over their souls. The whole psalm is built on the contrary-to-fact conditional. If God had not acted, this would have happened. But God did act, and so we are here, singing.

This is one of the most important habits the believer can cultivate. Look back at your life and ask, Where did God intervene? Where did things turn out differently than they could have? The Christian’s memory is not random. It is curated by the Spirit to recall the acts of God. Every time you remember a deliverance, you are doing what Psalm 124 does. You are putting words to what would have been, in order to celebrate what is.

The bird-and-snare image of verse 7 is one of the most evocative pictures of rescue in the Psalter. “We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped!” Anyone who has ever felt trapped, by sin, by circumstance, by fear, by depression, knows what this image describes. The snare is real. The bird really is caught. And then suddenly the snare breaks and the bird is in the air. That is what salvation feels like.

Psalm 125 then turns to the future. “Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever.” This is a remarkable promise. Those who trust in the LORD are themselves like Mount Zion, solid, enduring, eternal. Their faith is not just an internal feeling; it produces a kind of life that cannot be shaken. They become, in their very being, immovable.

And the image expands. “As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people.” Jerusalem is in the Judean hills, ringed by mountains on every side. The natural fortification was significant in ancient warfare. But the psalmist says God himself is the surrounding mountains around his people. Wherever the LORD’s people are, they are surrounded by his presence and protection. And this surrounding is permanent: from this time forth and forevermore.

The psalm is realistic about evil. The “scepter of wickedness” does come upon the land. But it will not rest there permanently. And the psalm closes with the simplest of prayers: “Peace be upon Israel!” Shalom, wholeness, flourishing, the fullness of God’s blessing.
connection: The Psalms of Ascent fit naturally with Jacob’s life. His life has been a pilgrimage, flight from home, years in Haran, return to Canaan, descent into Egypt to come. The believer’s life is similarly a pilgrimage. We are journeying through this age toward our true home. These psalms teach us how to walk: looking back in gratitude, looking forward in trust, surrounded by the presence of the LORD.
application:
Practice two habits today. First, the habit of Psalm 124: look back. Take a few minutes today to remember one specific way God intervened in your life. Maybe it was a near accident avoided. Maybe it was a relationship saved. Maybe it was a sin you almost committed but didn’t. Maybe it was a prayer answered just in time. Name it. Thank him for it. Tell someone about it.

Second, the habit of Psalm 125: trust. Receive the promise that you, trusting in the LORD, are like Mount Zion. You cannot be ultimately shaken. The same mountains that surround Jerusalem are the encircling presence of God around your life. Whatever feels unstable today, your foundation is not. Pray Psalm 125 over yourself: I trust in the LORD. I am like Mount Zion. He surrounds me. Peace be upon me, in his name.
prayerPrompts: Bless the LORD for a time he did not let you be overwhelmed, and tell him about it.
Thank him for the snares he has broken in your life.
Ask him to make your trust as settled as the mountains that surround Jerusalem.
